reason: The supplied polynomial argument incorrectly varies \(y\), although \(y\) is fixed. The repaired proof keeps \(y\) fixed and uses multiplicative orders and Dirichlet’s theorem.
text:
By Dirichlet’s theorem, choose a prime \(q\equiv1\pmod 4\) such that \(q>\max\{y,x+1\}\). Since \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(q\), choose \(s\) with \(s^2\equiv-1\pmod q\). As \(q\nmid y\), choose \(a\not\equiv0\pmod q\) satisfying \(ay\equiv s\pmod q\).

For every positive integer \(n\equiv a\pmod q\), we then have
\[
q\mid (ny)^2+1,
\]
so the hypothesis gives
\[
x^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
Because \(q>x\), let \(d=\operatorname{ord}_q(x)\). Thus \(d\mid\varphi(n)\) for every such \(n\), and \(d\mid q-1\).

Suppose \(d>2\). Since \(\gcd(d,q)=1\), the Chinese remainder theorem gives a reduced residue class \(c\pmod{qd}\) satisfying
\[
c\equiv a\pmod q,\qquad c\equiv-1\pmod d.
\]
By Dirichlet’s theorem, this class contains a prime \(r\). Taking \(n=r\), the preceding congruence implies
\[
d\mid\varphi(r)=r-1.
\]
But \(r\equiv-1\pmod d\), so \(r-1\equiv-2\pmod d\), forcing \(d\mid2\), a contradiction. Hence \(d\le2\), and therefore
\[
x^2\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
Thus \(q\mid(x-1)(x+1)\). Since \(1\le x<q-1\), this is possible only when \(x-1=0\). Consequently, \(x=1\).
